name: Isotretinoin gel (Isotrex)

lead: Isotretinoin gel, sold as Isotrex, is the topical form of isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid), applied directly to acne-prone skin. It is used to reduce inflamed and non-inflamed acne lesions, which improves how clear the skin looks.

Controlled trials from the 1990s and 2000s found 0.05% gel reduced lesions in mild to moderate acne compared with vehicle, with effects comparable to benzoyl peroxide and adapalene in head-to-head studies.

paras: It is a prescription gel applied to the affected skin; trials ran 12 weeks, with improvement building over that period. Isotrex is also listed as a brand in a combination product with erythromycin.[1] It is separate from oral isotretinoin used for severe cystic acne.[1]

Irritant dermatitis occurred in trials, though it was well tolerated by patients.[3] Adapalene was significantly better tolerated than isotretinoin gel in one comparison.[4] One 1991 study found negligible systemic availability even with excessive application.[7] Oral isotretinoin is contraindicated in pregnancy;[1] topical labeling should be consulted.

chain: Retinoid normalises follicle turnover and lowers inflammation
Fewer comedones and inflamed lesions over weeks
angle.text: It is used to treat acne so the skin looks clearer; in trials, lesion counts fell significantly versus vehicle by about 8-12 weeks.

lead: Isotretinoin gel 0.05% (Isotrex) is a topical retinoid developed for acne vulgaris. It contains isotretinoin, the same compound as the oral drug used for severe acne, but applied to the skin.[1]

A double-blind trial in 77 patients with mild to moderate acne compared isotretinoin gel, its vehicle and 5% benzoyl peroxide: vehicle had no effect, both actives reduced lesions, benzoyl peroxide worked faster on inflamed lesions, and isotretinoin showed significant improvement at 12 weeks.[2] An 80-patient trial found adapalene 0.1% and isotretinoin 0.05% were both highly effective, with adapalene better tolerated.[3]
Other studies tested it for melasma, Darier's disease and oral lichen planus,[4][5][6] and a Mexican trial compared it with topical retinoic acid for acne.[7]

paras: The main use is mild to moderate acne.[2][3][7] Trials also tested it for melasma, where it was compared with vehicle,[4] Darier's disease,[5] and oral lichen planus.[6]

Irritant dermatitis occurred equally with isotretinoin gel and benzoyl peroxide in one trial,[2] and adapalene was significantly better tolerated than isotretinoin gel.[3] A 1991 study found negligible systemic availability of retinoids with multiple, excessive applications.[8] Wikipedia notes oral isotretinoin is a known teratogen contraindicated in pregnancy.[1]

In a 12-week double-blind trial, isotretinoin gel significantly reduced inflamed and non-inflamed lesions versus vehicle and was comparable to benzoyl peroxide.[2] An open-label trial of 80 patients found it effective but less well tolerated than adapalene.[3] In a 40-week trial of 30 melasma patients, isotretinoin and vehicle with sunscreen both improved scores, with no significant difference between them.[4]
